explain.say: Your fingernails are made of the same tough protein as your hair, keratin. They grow from one place, hidden under the skin at the base of the nail.

explain.say: That place is the nail matrix. Its living cells divide all the time, and each new cell fills up with keratin, then flattens and dies, becoming part of a hard plate.

explain.say: New cells push older ones forward, so the nail plate slides slowly over the nail bed, the pink skin beneath, which is pink because of the blood vessels in it.

explain.say: The white tip that grows past your finger is dead keratin with no nerves, which is why trimming it doesn't hurt. Fingernails grow about 3 millimetres a month.

faq.a: From the nail matrix, a patch of living cells under the skin fold at the base of the nail. The pale half-moon you may see, the lunula, is the visible front of the matrix.
asks: Tell me about the nail matrix

faq.q: Why doesn't it hurt to cut your nails?
faq.a: The nail plate is made of dead, keratin-filled cells with no nerves or blood vessels, so trimming the free edge doesn't hurt.
asks: Tell me about the free edge

faq.a: The nail bed is the skin under the nail plate. It is rich in blood vessels, which make it look pink, and it holds the nail in place as it slides forward.
asks: Tell me about the nail sliding over the bed

faq.a: Fingernails grow about 3 millimetres a month, and a whole fingernail takes about six months to replace. Toenails grow more slowly, roughly 1 millimetre a month.
asks: Do fingernails grow faster than toenails?

faq.a: The cuticle is a thin layer of skin at the base of the nail that seals the gap between the nail and the skin, helping keep germs out of the matrix.

facts: Fingernails grow about 3 millimetres a month; toenails about 1 millimetre a month.
Nails are made of keratin, the same protein family as hair.
